\chapter{Case Endings and Dative Subjects}
\label{ch:ml-dative-case}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I know Malayalam the way Malayalam itself builds it -- with no subject at all, marking myself with the dative -ikku.}

Say enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām, set it against ñān malayāḷam saṁsārikkunnu, and stack the dative's four Dravidian cousins.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-ikku]{-\ml{ിക്ക്} (-ikku) — \textquotedblleft{}to, for\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C06-dative-ikku}



\begin{quote}
Your first \textbf{case ending}. English puts \textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{} in \textbf{front} as its own word. Malayalam sticks it on the \textbf{back} — and that is the biggest structural fact about the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{+ dative} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\ml{പേര്} \emph{pēru} — name & \ml{പേര}\textbf{\ml{ിന്}} \emph{pēr\textbf{inu}} & to/for the name \\
\ml{ജോലി} \emph{jōli} — work & \ml{ജോലി}\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \emph{jōli\textbf{kku}} & for work \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Malayalam's dative has two shapes — \textbf{-\ml{ിക്ക്}} \emph{-ikku} and \textbf{-\ml{ിന്}} \emph{-inu} — chosen by the sound the noun ends in. Same case, same job; the seam is still visible.

And with \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}, which reshapes first:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} \emph{ñān} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku} (\textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

Learn \emph{enikku} cold — it opens a great many everyday Malayalam sentences, as the next lesson shows.

\begin{culture}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Malayalam \textbf{-ikku}} & \textbf{a Latin ending like \textbf{-īs}} \\
\midrule
pins down the case? & \textbf{yes} — dative, always & \textbf{no} — \emph{-īs} is dative \textbf{or} ablative \\
carries number? & \textbf{no} — a separate suffix does & yes — plural, baked in \\
carries declension class? & \textbf{no} & yes — 1st/2nd only \\
can you see the seam? & \textbf{yes}: \emph{jōli} + \emph{kku} & no — one fused lump \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Malayalam \textbf{stacks}: each suffix means one thing and sits in a fixed order — so a long word can be read piece by piece. Latin \textbf{fuses}: \emph{-īs} is case \emph{and} plural \emph{and} declension at once, indivisible, and it doesn't even settle \emph{which} case. Malayalam's dative is never ambiguous.

That's what \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{agglutinative}\textquotedblright{} means, and why Malayalam words grow long without growing hard: they are \textbf{built}, not memorised.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\emph{pēru} … \emph{pērinu}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\emph{ñān} … \emph{enikku}\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\emph{jōlikku}\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}for work,\textquotedblright{} from Ch. 5's \ml{ജോലി}
  \item the principle — \textquotedblleft{}one suffix, one meaning, visible seam\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\ml{ിക്ക്}} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To}\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{for}.\textquotedblright{}) Where does it go? (\textbf{On the end} of the noun.) What is \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku}.) Why does the suffix have two shapes? (\textbf{-ikku} and \textbf{-inu} are chosen by the noun's ending — one case, two forms.) How is that unlike a Latin ending? (Latin \textbf{fuses} case+number+declension — and \emph{-īs} doesn't even fix \emph{which} case; Malayalam's carries \textbf{one} meaning, unambiguously, seam visible.) Next: the sentence where the person isn't the subject.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām]{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം} — \textquotedblleft{}I know Malayalam\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C06-dative-subject}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 5 gave you \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} speak Malayalam.\textquotedblright{} Now say \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{know} Malayalam.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam will not let you use \emph{ñān}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}.} \emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām.} literally: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to-me} Malayalam is-knowable.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}} \emph{enikku} & \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{} — the dative from the last lesson \\
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളം}} \emph{malayāḷam} & Malayalam (Ch. 5) \\
\textbf{\ml{അറിയാം}} \emph{aṟiyām} & \textquotedblleft{}can be known\textquotedblright{} — \emph{aṟiy-} \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{-ām}, the \emph{able-to} ending \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{You are not the subject.} \emph{Ñān} is gone; the person has been moved into the dative, and the sentence is now about the \textbf{language}. Malayalam isn't saying you perform an act of knowing — it's saying the language is knowable \textbf{to you}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Malayalam separates what you \textbf{do} from what \textbf{happens to} you. Speaking is an action, so Ch. 5 used \emph{ñān}. But knowing, liking, wanting, being hungry — these \textbf{arrive} at you. Malayalam marks that by putting the person in the \textbf{dative}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English frames it as} & \textbf{Malayalam frames it as} \\
\midrule
I \textbf{know} Malayalam & Malayalam is known \textbf{to me} \\
I \textbf{like} it & it is pleasing \textbf{to me} \\
I \textbf{am} cold & cold is \textbf{to me} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English preserves one fossil of exactly this: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{methinks}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{me} is a dative, \textquotedblleft{}it seems \textbf{to me}.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam made it the rule.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I know {[}the language{]}\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{the dative} \\
\midrule
Malayalam & \emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām} & \textbf{-ikku} \\
Tamil & \emph{enakku tamiḻ teriyum} & \textbf{-ukku} \\
Telugu & \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} & \textbf{-ku} \\
Kannada & \emph{nanage kannaḍa gottu} & \textbf{-ge} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at the first column: Malayalam's \emph{enikku} and Tamil's \emph{enakku} are nearly the \textbf{same word} — the two languages separated most recently of the four, and it shows. One construction, four languages, four visibly related suffixes: the Dravidian family showing its bones, as \emph{blanc/bianco/branco} did for Romance.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{ñān malayāḷam saṁsārikkunnu}\textquotedblright{} (I speak) … \textquotedblleft{}\emph{enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām}\textquotedblright{} (known to me)
  \item the near-twins — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{enikku} … \emph{enakku}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four cousins — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{-ikku · -ukku · -ku · -ge}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}} literally say? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To-me} Malayalam \textbf{is-knowable}.\textquotedblright{}) What has English got that Malayalam hasn't? (A nominative \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān} is replaced by the dative \emph{enikku}.) Why the dative? (Knowing \textbf{happens to} you.) Which Tamil word is \emph{enikku} almost identical to, and why? (\textbf{Enakku} — Tamil and Malayalam split most recently of the four.) Which English word keeps the same idea? (\textbf{Methinks}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ka]{\ml{ക} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S01-letter-ka}



\begin{quote}
Highly rounded and loopy — full circles, hooks and curls, with almost no straight lines.

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ക}}
\textbf{\ml{ക}} — \emph{ka}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{k}, it is \textbf{ka}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{ക} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}} \emph{nāḷe kāṇāṁ} — see you tomorrow
  \item \textbf{\ml{താമസിക്കുക}} \emph{tāmasikkuka} — to live, to stay
  \item \textbf{\ml{ജോലി} \ml{ചെയ്യുക}} \emph{jōli ceyyuka} — to work (lit. \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ക} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ക} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{ക} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}  ·  \ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}  ·  \ml{നന്ദി}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{ക} three times, saying \emph{ka} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{ക} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{ക}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ka}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
